newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP suggests less slack in economy, higher rates.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP suggests less slack in economy, higher rates.

text.p: A small upward revision in first quarter UK GDP, and hefty upward revisions to growth figures covering the last three years, mean there is less slack in the economy than previously thought and interest rates will soon head higher, analysts said.

"We previously thought there was an output gap in the economy of around 1.25 percent last quarter, but taking into account the revisions to the historical profile of GDP we are cutting that to 0.25 percent," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"It reduces still further the room for error the Bank of England has on interest rates and makes it a tough call at the July meeting."
The Bank's monetary policy committee will decided whether or not to raise rates again on July 10, just over a week after the July 2 budget. Barty forecasts it will hold fire in July.
"There will probably be some modest fiscal tightening in the budget, and sterling reaching ever new highs is a big problem facing the Bank. I think they'll skip July and raise in August."
Figures released on Friday showed the British economy grew by an unrevised 0.9 percent in the first quarter of 1996 compared with the previous three months.
Compared with the same period last year, growth was 3.1 percent higher, revised up from 3.0 percent at the previous estimate.

But there were chunky revisions to data going back to 1994. That showed GDP growth was 4.5 percent in 1994 compared with a previous estimate of 4.0 percent, and was 2.8 percent in 1995 compared with a previous estimate of 2.5 percent.
Growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 was also revised up, to 2.9 percent year-on-year from 2.6 percent at the last estimate.

These big revisions have reawakened fears that UK GDP data are again suspect. In the late 1980s, the data continually underestimated expenditure, which some commentators said mislead the then Chancellor of the Exchequer Nigel Lawson into keeping fiscal and monetary policy too loose.

"Upward revisions to previous years' data have left the level of GDP about one percent higher than previously estimated and will doubtless rekindle fears that official figures are once again understating the true strength of the uptrend," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
But he said the most up-to-date first quarter data paint a rather weaker picture of growth than previously estimates.
"Investment was revised down sharply and even consumer spending was a touch weaker," he noted.
Domestic expenditure grew 0.7 percent quarter-on quarter compared with 1.2 percent estimated previously.

And surprisingly, real disposable income fell by 0.2 percent in the quarter. This was mainly due to a drop in the 'other income' component -- largely comprising interest and dividends -- along with a big surge in the tax take during the quarter, up 4.4 percent. The ONS said the run up to the introduction of self assessment on tax returns may have been responsible.
But even if income growth does turn out to be weaker, this should be offset by a rise in other forms of wealth.
"Rising wealth, in the form of higher house prices and windfall payouts is likely to keep spending robust," said Loynes.
